surveyMeta.focalPoint: Steward survey — the environment the neighborhood depends on (Block F), who works with whom (Block G), and the center's own record (Block H, answered once per wave by the record-keeper). Rate the eleven spheres as you see them first.

nodeLabels.S-6: ABILITY TO GET THINGS DONE WITHIN THE NHOOD

nodeDescriptions.S-1:
_S-1 is the integration function — the neighborhood's capacity to connect its parts into coherent collective action rather than a collection of separate efforts._
**Our neighborhood's people, groups, and initiatives are aware of each other, working in alignment, and not duplicating or undermining each other's efforts.**
nodeDescriptions.S-2:
_S-2 is the participation function — the breadth and depth of who is actually engaged in neighborhood life, not just present in it._
**Our neighborhood draws people in. Residents, organizations, and newcomers find meaningful ways to contribute, and no one who wants to participate is left out.**
nodeDescriptions.S-3:
_S-3 is the infrastructure function — the physical spaces, digital tools, and shared resources that make it possible for people to work together effectively._
**Our neighborhood has the spaces, tools, and shared resources people need to meet, organize, communicate, and get things done together.**
nodeDescriptions.S-4:
_S-4 is the community-facing awareness function — knowing who is here, what they need, and how to reach them._
**We know our neighbors, what they need from us, what they can contribute, and how to communicate with them.**
nodeDescriptions.S-5:
_S-5 is the adaptive function — the neighborhood's capacity to notice what is and isn't working, take that seriously, and actually change course._
**Our neighborhood learns from experience. We notice what is working and what isn't, we talk about it honestly, and we use what we learn to do better.**
nodeDescriptions.S-6:
_S-6 is the execution function — the neighborhood's actual capacity to follow through on intentions and turn plans and commitments into completed work._
**Our neighborhood can turn decisions into action. When we commit to something, we have the people, coordination, and follow-through to actually make it happen.**
nodeDescriptions.S-7:
_S-7 is the resource function — the flow of money, funding, and material support that sustains neighborhood activity and makes sustained effort possible._
**Our neighborhood has enough financial resources to sustain the work we care about. Resources are raised, managed, and distributed in ways people trust.**
nodeDescriptions.S-8:
_S-8 is the planning function — the neighborhood's capacity to think ahead, set intentions, coordinate future action._
**Our neighborhood makes plans that are realistic, shared, and actually guide what we do together.**
nodeDescriptions.S-9:
S-9 is the external awareness function — sensing and communicating with the larger environment beyond the neighborhood boundary.
**Our neighborhood understands what is going on  around us. We know our supporters as well as extractors.**
nodeDescriptions.S-10:
_S-10 is the self-organizing capacity — the neighborhood's ability to actually mobilize around problems and opportunities as they arise._ 
**Our neighborhood can self-organize to understand and solve our problems and take advantage of opportunities.**
nodeDescriptions.S-11:
_S-11 is the values-in-action function — the actual norms, habits, and shared expectations that shape how people treat each other and what they believe is possible together._
**Our neighborhood has a culture of mutual respect, honest conversation, and shared responsibility. How we treat each other reflects what we say we believe.**

edgeDescriptions.1->2: _Does coordination make it easier for more people to find their place and get involved?_ **When the neighborhood's efforts are well-coordinated, people can find their entry point and contribute without duplicating work or falling through the cracks.**
edgeDescriptions.2->1: _Does broad, deep involvement make it easier to coordinate across the neighborhood?_ **When more people are genuinely engaged, coordination becomes richer — more perspectives are in the room, more connections are made, and collective action becomes more possible.**
edgeDescriptions.3->1: _Do shared tools and workspaces enable better coordination?_ **When people have the right spaces to meet and the right tools to communicate, coordinating across the neighborhood becomes practical rather than aspirational.**
edgeDescriptions.9->10: _Does our collective awareness of the outside world actually sharpen how we organize ourselves to act?_ **Our neighborhood's awareness of outside forces, opportunities, and threats is actively shaping how we come together to solve problems and take advantage of opportunities.**
edgeDescriptions.10->9: _Does active neighborhood self-organization focus and sharpen what outside information we seek and use?_ **When our neighborhood comes together around a problem or opportunity, we get better at knowing what outside information we need.**
edgeDescriptions.8->10:
_Does neighborhood planning actually enable and focus our collective capacity to act, rather than replacing it?_
**Our neighborhood planning gives people the context and direction they need to step up and organize around real problems and opportunities.**
edgeDescriptions.10->8:
_Does our lived experience of working together actually improve the quality of our planning?_
**When our neighborhood comes together to act, what we learn shapes and improves our plans.**
edgeDescriptions.8->9:
_Does our neighborhood planning actively direct what we look for and pay attention to beyond our boundaries?_
**Our neighborhood's plans and priorities are actively shaping what outside information we seek out and pay attention to.**
edgeDescriptions.9->8:
_Does our awareness of the outside world actually update and improve our neighborhood's plans?_
**What we learn about the world beyond our neighborhood is regularly finding its way into how we plan and set priorities.**
edgeDescriptions.1->4: _Does coordination across the neighborhood deepen how well we know who is here and what they need?_ **When the neighborhood's people and groups work in alignment, we get better at knowing our neighbors — who they are, what they bring, and what they need from us.**
edgeDescriptions.1->3: _Does coordination drive investment in the shared tools and spaces that make collaboration possible?_ **When our neighborhood coordinates well, we identify what tools and workspaces we actually need and make sure they are available to everyone.**
edgeDescriptions.2->3: _Does the breadth of involvement shape what tools and spaces the neighborhood develops?_ **When a wide range of people are involved, the tools and spaces we build reflect actual needs rather than the preferences of a narrow group.**
edgeDescriptions.2->4: _Does broad involvement deepen the neighborhood's knowledge of itself?_ **When more people participate, we collectively know more about who lives here, what people need, and what resources and capacities exist among us.**
edgeDescriptions.2->5: _Does the range of who is involved improve the quality of the neighborhood's learning?_ **When diverse people are genuinely engaged, the neighborhood hears more honest feedback, catches blind spots earlier, and learns faster from both success and failure.**
edgeDescriptions.2->6: _Does involvement translate into actual capacity to execute?_ **When people are genuinely engaged, the neighborhood has more hands, more skills, and more follow-through to turn commitments into completed work.**
edgeDescriptions.2->7: _Does broad involvement strengthen the neighborhood's resource base?_ **When more people are engaged, the neighborhood is better positioned to attract funding, generate in-kind contributions, and steward resources with broad accountability.**
edgeDescriptions.3->2: _Do shared tools and accessible workspaces lower the barriers to participation?_ **When spaces are welcoming and tools are easy to use, more people can find their way into neighborhood life — especially those who might otherwise be left out.**
edgeDescriptions.3->4: _Do shared tools and workspaces help the neighborhood know itself better?_ **Good tools for communication and shared spaces for gathering help us stay current on who is here, what is happening, and what people need.**
edgeDescriptions.3->5: _Do shared tools and workspaces support honest reflection and real learning?_ **When people have good places to meet and share information, the neighborhood can have the kinds of conversations that lead to genuine learning and course correction.**
edgeDescriptions.3->6: _Do shared tools and workspaces increase the neighborhood's execution capacity?_ **When people have what they need to organize and work together, getting things done becomes less dependent on heroic individual effort and more supported by shared infrastructure.**
edgeDescriptions.3->11: _Do the tools and spaces we build reflect and reinforce the values we hold?_ **The spaces we create and the tools we adopt send a message about who belongs and how we work together. Inclusive, accessible infrastructure builds an inclusive, accessible culture.**
edgeDescriptions.4->1: _Does knowing our neighbors well make it easier to coordinate across the neighborhood?_ **When we know who is here, what they do, and what they care about, coordination becomes more targeted — we connect the right people to the right efforts.**
edgeDescriptions.4->2: _Does deep internal awareness help us draw more people into participation?_ **When we know our neighbors — their interests, capacities, and barriers — we can reach out in ways that actually resonate and make involvement feel possible for more people.**
edgeDescriptions.4->3: _Does knowing what people need shape what tools and spaces we build?_ **When we understand who is here and how they work, we can design and maintain tools and spaces that actually serve the full range of people in the neighborhood.**
edgeDescriptions.4->5: _Does knowing our neighbors deeply improve the quality of how we learn and adapt?_ **When we have honest knowledge of who is here and how things are going for them, we have better raw material for learning — closer to what is actually true rather than what we assume.**
edgeDescriptions.4->7: _Does internal awareness make the neighborhood more capable of acting effectively?_ **Knowing who can do what — and who needs what — means we can mobilize the right people and resources when action is needed, rather than working blind.**
edgeDescriptions.4->11: _Does genuine knowledge of our neighbors shape the kind of community we become?_ **When we actually know each other — not just as categories but as people — the neighborhood develops a culture of real relationship rather than surface-level coexistence.**
edgeDescriptions.5->2: _Does the neighborhood's capacity to learn and change make participation more meaningful?_ **When people see that the neighborhood actually learns from feedback and changes course, they are more likely to stay engaged — their participation feels like it matters.**
edgeDescriptions.5->3: _Does learning from experience improve how we develop and maintain our shared tools and spaces?_ **When we reflect honestly on what is and isn't working, we update our tools and spaces to better serve actual needs rather than perpetuating what has always been done.**
edgeDescriptions.5->4: _Does the neighborhood's learning process deepen its knowledge of who is here and what they need?_ **Honest reflection surfaces gaps in what we know about our neighbors. Good learning processes reveal who we have been missing and what we have been misunderstanding.**
edgeDescriptions.5->6: _Does learning from experience make the neighborhood more effective at executing?_ **When we learn from what has worked and what hasn't, we get better at turning commitments into results — less wasted effort, more targeted action.**
edgeDescriptions.5->7: _Does the quality of the neighborhood's learning strengthen its resource base?_ **When we can demonstrate honest reflection and adaptive management, funders and contributors are more willing to invest. Learning is what makes trust sustainable over time.**
edgeDescriptions.5->8: _Does the neighborhood's learning actually feed back into better planning?_ **When we learn from experience — from both successes and failures — that knowledge improves the plans we make. Plans grounded in real learning are more realistic and more shared.**
edgeDescriptions.5->9: _Does strong internal learning sharpen how we attend to and use outside information?_ **A neighborhood that learns well from its own experience also gets better at knowing what outside information matters and how to make use of it.**
edgeDescriptions.5->11: _Does the neighborhood's capacity for honest learning shape its culture?_ **When a neighborhood can acknowledge mistakes, celebrate growth, and change course together, it builds a culture of honesty and shared accountability rather than defensiveness.**
edgeDescriptions.6->2: _Does the neighborhood's ability to deliver on commitments attract and sustain involvement?_ **When people see that things actually get done, they stay engaged. Demonstrated effectiveness is one of the most powerful invitations to participate.**
edgeDescriptions.6->3: _Does getting things done generate investment in the tools and spaces needed to sustain that capacity?_ **As the neighborhood accomplishes things together, it learns what infrastructure it needs and builds the case for maintaining and improving shared tools and workspaces.**
edgeDescriptions.6->5: _Does the experience of getting things done generate the neighborhood's best learning?_ **Working together on real tasks reveals what we know and what we don't, what works and what doesn't. Execution is where the neighborhood's learning happens most concretely.**
edgeDescriptions.6->8: _Does the experience of getting things done improve the quality of the neighborhood's planning?_ **Plans made by people who have worked together on real things are better — more grounded, more realistic, more attentive to what actually matters.**
edgeDescriptions.6->7: _Does the neighborhood's track record of getting things done strengthen its resource base?_ **Demonstrated capacity to execute attracts funding and in-kind support. When people can see that the neighborhood delivers, they are more willing to invest in it.**
edgeDescriptions.6->10: _Does the experience of getting things done together develop and reveal neighborhood leadership?_ **Working on real tasks together is where people discover their own capacity and others discover it in them. Execution is where leadership grows.**
edgeDescriptions.6->11: _Does getting things done together shape the neighborhood's culture?_ **Shared accomplishment builds confidence, trust, and a sense of collective identity. A neighborhood that does things together develops a culture of we can.**
edgeDescriptions.7->2: _Does having adequate resources make involvement more accessible and sustainable?_ **When the neighborhood has resources, it can reduce barriers to participation — covering costs, compensating time, and making it possible for people who cannot volunteer freely to stay engaged.**
edgeDescriptions.7->4: _Does adequate resourcing enable the neighborhood to know itself better?_ **With resources, the neighborhood can invest in the outreach, listening, and relationship-building needed to actually know who is here, especially those who are hardest to reach.**
edgeDescriptions.7->5: _Does adequate resourcing support the neighborhood's capacity to learn and change?_ **Learning takes time and attention. When the neighborhood has resources, it can invest in honest reflection, evaluation, and the conversations needed to adapt and improve.**
edgeDescriptions.7->6: _Do financial resources translate into execution capacity?_ **Resources enable action — paying for materials, compensating labor, sustaining effort over time. A neighborhood with adequate resources can follow through on what it commits to.**
edgeDescriptions.7->9: _Does having resources improve the neighborhood's capacity to engage with the world beyond its boundaries?_ **Resources make it possible to attend events, build external relationships, hire expertise, and engage with the broader environment in ways that voluntary effort alone cannot sustain.**
edgeDescriptions.7->11: _Does the way resources flow through the neighborhood reflect and shape its culture?_ **How money is raised, managed, and distributed is a direct expression of neighborhood values. Transparent, equitable resource stewardship builds trust and reinforces a culture of shared ownership.**
edgeDescriptions.7->10: _Does having adequate resources enable and sustain neighborhood leadership?_ **Leadership without resources burns people out. When the neighborhood can compensate, support, and develop its leaders, leadership becomes more sustainable and more broadly distributed.**
edgeDescriptions.8->5: _Does the quality of neighborhood planning create conditions for genuine learning?_ **Good plans include honest assessment of what worked before. When plans are made with reflection built in, the neighborhood gets better at learning from experience rather than just moving on.**
edgeDescriptions.8->6: _Does good neighborhood planning actually increase the capacity to execute?_ **Clear, shared, realistic plans reduce confusion and duplication. When people know what the priorities are and who is doing what, getting things done becomes more possible.**
edgeDescriptions.8->11: _Does the way the neighborhood plans together reflect and reinforce its culture?_ **A planning process that is open, honest, and inclusive builds a culture of shared ownership. When people help shape the plans, they are more likely to feel responsible for carrying them out.**
edgeDescriptions.9->5: _Does awareness of the outside world enrich the neighborhood's learning?_ **Knowing what is happening beyond our boundaries — what other neighborhoods have tried, what forces are shaping our environment — gives the neighborhood richer material to learn from.**
edgeDescriptions.9->7: _Does awareness of the outside world improve the neighborhood's ability to attract and manage resources?_ **Knowing what funders are prioritizing, what programs are available, and what the broader landscape looks like helps the neighborhood position itself to attract and sustain the resources it needs.**
edgeDescriptions.9->11: _Does awareness of the world beyond the neighborhood shape its internal culture?_ **Knowing what is happening elsewhere — both threats and possibilities — helps the neighborhood develop a culture that is confident and grounded rather than fearful or parochial.**
edgeDescriptions.10->6: _Does neighborhood self-organization translate into actual execution capacity?_ **When the neighborhood can mobilize around problems and opportunities, things actually get done. Leadership that is distributed and responsive is what turns energy into results.**
edgeDescriptions.10->7: _Does active neighborhood self-organization strengthen the resource base?_ **When people are organizing around real issues, they generate the energy, visibility, and credibility that attract funding, in-kind support, and the contributions of time and skill.**
edgeDescriptions.10->11: _Does the way the neighborhood self-organizes shape its culture?_ **Who steps up, who is welcomed in, and how people organize together sends a constant signal about what the neighborhood values and who belongs. Leadership practice is culture in action.**
edgeDescriptions.11->3: _Does the neighborhood's culture shape what tools and spaces it builds and how they are maintained?_ **A culture of inclusion and shared ownership produces tools and spaces that are accessible to everyone and maintained by everyone. Culture determines whether shared infrastructure is cared for or neglected.**
edgeDescriptions.11->4: _Does the neighborhood's culture affect how well it knows itself?_ **A culture of honest conversation and genuine curiosity about neighbors produces richer, more accurate internal knowledge. A closed or defensive culture produces blind spots.**
edgeDescriptions.11->5: _Does the neighborhood's culture enable or inhibit genuine learning and change?_ **Learning requires honesty about failure and openness to being wrong. A culture of psychological safety — where people can speak honestly without fear — is the precondition for real learning.**
edgeDescriptions.11->6: _Does the neighborhood's culture affect its capacity to follow through and execute?_ **A culture of shared responsibility and mutual accountability means people show up, follow through, and cover for each other. Culture is what makes collective execution possible or impossible.**
edgeDescriptions.11->7: _Does the neighborhood's culture affect its ability to attract and steward resources?_ **Funders and contributors want to invest in communities with healthy cultures — where accountability is real, relationships are genuine, and resources will be used well. Culture is what makes the neighborhood trustworthy.**
edgeDescriptions.11->8: _Does the neighborhood's culture affect the quality of its planning?_ **A culture that values honesty and shared ownership produces planning processes that surface real issues, hear dissenting voices, and generate plans people actually believe in.**
edgeDescriptions.11->9: _Does the neighborhood's culture shape how it engages with the outside world?_ **A confident, grounded neighborhood culture enables engagement with outside forces without being captured or overwhelmed by them. Culture is what makes external engagement generative rather than threatening.**
edgeDescriptions.11->10: _Does the neighborhood's culture shape who leads and how?_ **Culture determines whether leadership is hoarded or distributed, whether stepping up is welcomed or punished, whether new voices find their way in. A healthy culture grows leaders constantly.**

extraItems.text: **In the last three months, which neighborhood groups, projects or initiatives did you actually work with — not just hear about?** _List them, one per line, using the names on the roster where you can._
extraItems.help: Working with means you did something together: a meeting you both attended for a purpose, a task you shared, a hand-off. Hearing about them or reading their posts does not count.
extraItems.blockHelp: Two questions about who you actually work with. Names are used only to draw the network; the report shows counts and shapes, never who named whom. In anonymous mode the names are replaced by codes before anything is stored.
extraItems.derives: Density among active groups → S-1; your number of ties → S-2; components → fragmentation

extraItems.text: **If something went wrong on your block tomorrow — a flood, an eviction notice, a fight — who would you go to first?** _Name up to three people or groups._
extraItems.help: Answer with who you would really go to, not who you think you should. A group name is fine if that is how you would reach them.

extraItems.text: **Joint activities.** _How many activities in the last three months were carried out by two or more neighborhood groups together?_
extraItems.blockHelp: Eleven counts, one per sphere, for the last three months, answered once per wave by the person who keeps the center's records — not by every resident. Each is the observed side of a sphere the survey otherwise measures only as belief. Enter whole numbers; where two numbers are asked for, enter both.
extraItems.gaming: Counting every meeting as joint; define joint as shared work, not shared attendance.
